result.competitor: I found no dedicated host-compliance software or service for St Kitts and Nevis. However, the free IRD SMARTS system, reached through the My Government Portal, already handles online VAT filing and payment, which is the core filing job. Local accountants and property managers are the other alternative; none were found by name. The search was English-only, which is the local language.
result.duty: The duty is real. IRD guidance dated 30 Dec 2024 says hosts on Airbnb, Booking, Vrbo, Expedia and similar platforms must register and declare rental income under the VAT Act Cap 18.47 and the Island Enhancement Fund Act Cap 20.51. There was a voluntary window to 28 Feb 2025 and full enforcement from 1 Jan 2025 (IRD press pages and KPMG, seen in search snippets). Accommodation takes the 10% reduced VAT rate under s.27(1)(d). The standard rate went back to 17% on 1 Jul 2025. VAT registration applies above a reported turnover threshold of XCD 96,000. Only a tax aggregator gives that figure; IRD did not confirm it. On Nevis, the Tourism Development Levy of 3% of gross sales is due by the 15th of each month, per KPMG. The Amenities for Tourists (Amendment) Bill 2025 passed in the Nevis Island Assembly on 6 Mar 2025. An NIA article from Apr 2026 says the rise to 3% happened in 2023, which conflicts with the 2025 date. Penalty amounts were not found. The IRD and KPMG pages returned 404 on fetch, so the duty facts come from search snippets.
result.market: AirDNA counts about 840 active short-term rental listings in the whole federation as of June 2026, across Airbnb, Vrbo and Booking. Other trackers count 163 to 377. Many hosts run several listings, so the number of distinct hosts is likely a few hundred. Average revenue per listing is about USD 28.8k (about XCD 78k), which is below the reported XCD 96k VAT threshold. That suggests many hosts may not need to register for VAT at all. The market is very small.
result.reason: The duty is real and recurring: monthly VAT and IEF returns, plus the monthly Nevis TDL. But the market is tiny. There are about 840 listings and probably only a few hundred hosts, and many may fall under the reported XCD 96k VAT threshold. The free IRD SMARTS portal already covers e-filing and payment, so software would only add calculation and reminders on top. Hosts with enough revenue are likely to use a local accountant or property manager. Willingness to pay for a niche SaaS in a federation of about 47,000 people is low, and there is too little revenue for a solo founder even with full coverage. It might work as a feature inside a broader Eastern Caribbean host-compliance tool, but not on its own.

result.competitor: I found no local or regional product made for small DNFBPs in St Kitts and Nevis. The search returned only generic or foreign tools, such as Shufti Pro KYC/ID verification for SKN documents and UAE DNFBP AML suites. I could not confirm whether the FIU runs a free STR portal such as goAML. The regulator publishes guidelines, but I saw no templates or portal on the FSRC DNFBP page. The competitor search was limited (2 queries).
result.duty: Real, but the details are unconfirmed. The FSRC St Kitts law library lists 'SRO No. 17 of 2026 DNFBP Regulations' and 'Guidelines for DNFBPs'. The Nevis FSRC lists the 'Financial Services (DNFBP) Regulations (No.17 of 2026)', the AML/CFT Guidelines for DNFBPs and the 'FSRC (Administrative Penalties) Regulations, 2026 (No.14 of 2026)'. The duty is not new. The Proceeds of Crime Act Cap 4.28 already made failure to report suspicion an offence, the AML Regulations 2011 apply, the Nevis DNFBP guidelines date from 2019, and the 2018 amendments required accountants and lawyers doing financial business to be licensed by the FSRC. The SRO 17 PDF and the 2019 guidelines PDF would not render as text, so I could not confirm the covered sectors (real estate, jewellers), any registration deadline or the penalty amounts. Frequency is ongoing: CDD per client, records, STRs when suspicion arises, and periodic risk assessments.
result.market: Not reached. Neither the FSRC pages nor my searches gave a count of DNFBPs. The 2022 CFATF MER PDF, which probably has sector counts, would not render as text. The federation has about 50k people, so covered firms probably number in the low hundreds at most (my estimate, unverified).
result.reason: The DNFBP AML duty is real and backed by a new 2026 instrument, SRO 17, plus an administrative penalties regime. It is not a new obligation, though, because POCA, the AML Regulations 2011 and the 2019 DNFBP guidelines already applied. I could not read the sectors, deadlines or penalties in SRO 17. The market is very small, likely a few hundred firms or fewer, and lawyers and accountants may already use global AML or KYC tools. Willingness to pay among tiny local jewellers and real estate agents is doubtful. An MVP (CDD forms, risk assessment template, STR log) is simple, but the total revenue ceiling in SKN is very low. It only makes sense as part of a pan-ECCU or OECS DNFBP kit.

Duty is real. The Nevis Companies Registry notice (4 Mar 2026) required annual returns by 31 Mar 2026. Fees were $150 for local companies and $100 for external ones. The late penalty is $250 per month. The St Kitts FSRC lists annual fees of USD 100 for a private company. Beneficial ownership records appear to sit with registered agents, not a public filing, but sources conflict and I did not check the statute. Competition: registered agents and compliance sellers such as Expanship already sell this, and the filings are low-volume, so the market is small. Buyers are served by agents. I did not find the St Kitts deadline, penalty text or a company count. Weak SaaS fit, so the score stays at 3.

Duty is real: the NGO Act Cap 20.59, amended 2020 and 2024, requires annual accounts (audited, with a lower-revenue unaudited option in the 2024 bill) and an activities report to the Registrar. The FSRC has AML inspection powers, and deregistration is possible with a $150 reinstatement fee. The bill text showed a $100 per month late fine, which I couldn't confirm was enacted. No exact deadline or NGO count was found. The only existing tool is the FSRC's free xlsx form and PDF statement. I found no commercial competitor, but I didn't search for one. The market is tiny (a small island nation, probably a few hundred NGOs), buyers are volunteers with little willingness to pay, and the penalties are low. Hence a low score.

result.duty: Licensees must record plants, batches and every financial transaction in the Authority's national tracking system (Cannabis (Medicinal Cannabis Licensing) Regulations SRO 17 of 2022, reg. 55). I found no penalty or frequency detail.
result.market: No licences reported issued as of early September 2026. Nine licence categories exist. The market is probably a handful to a few dozen licensees.
result.reason: The duty is real. The Cannabis (Medicinal Cannabis Licensing) Regulations, SRO 17 of 2022, made under the Cannabis Act 2020, set nine licence categories and require transactions to be logged in a national tracking system. But the Authority has already commissioned GrowerIQ to build and run that mandated national system, per an August 2026 vendor press release. The state system does the core seed-to-sale job, so a third-party product has no opening. No licence issuance was reported yet, so the buyer count is near zero, and the licensee market is tiny. The activity is also not clearly recurring. The statute name is unclear: sources say both "Cannabis Act 2020" and "Medicinal Cannabis Industry Act". I did not open the regulation text, and the GrowerIQ details come from the vendor's own press release.
